knowledge_graph.title: Radiation therapy
knowledge_graph.description: Radiation therapy or radiotherapy is a treatment using ionizing radiation, generally provided as part of cancer therapy to either kill or control the growth of malignant cells. It is normally delivered by a linear particle accelerator.

related_questions.question: How long do you have to stay away from someone after radiation?

text_blocks.snippet: For most types of radiation therapy, you can resume normal contact with others immediately after treatment, especially with external beam radiation. However, if you've received internal radiation or systemic radiation, you might need to limit close contact with certain individuals for a short period, typically up to a week. It's crucial to consult with your healthcare team for specific guidelines, as the duration and precautions vary based on the type of radiation and the treatment plan.

list.title: External Beam Radiation:
list.snippet: This type of radiation, where a machine directs beams of radiation at the tumor, does not make the patient radioactive. You can safely be around others immediately after treatment.

list.title: Internal Radiation (Brachytherapy):
list.snippet: With internal radiation, a radioactive source is placed inside the body (either temporarily or permanently).
If the source is removed after treatment, you can usually resume normal contact relatively quickly.

If the source is left in place, your doctor will provide specific instructions on how long to maintain distance from others, particularly pregnant women and young children. This period could be a few weeks to a couple of months.

list.title: Systemic Radiation:
list.snippet: This involves radioactive substances administered intravenously, and they can cause the patient to be radioactive for a short time.

You may need to limit close contact with others for a few days after treatment, and you might need to follow specific hygiene practices like using the toilet sitting down and washing hands thoroughly after using the restroom.
Avoid sharing utensils, towels, or clothing, and consider sleeping in a separate bed.
You may need to avoid sexual contact for a week or longer and use condoms, says Drugs.com.
It's important to drink plenty of fluids to help flush the radioactive material out of your system.

list.title: Consult with your doctor:
list.snippet: Always follow the specific instructions provided by your radiation oncologist or healthcare team.

list.title: Protect vulnerable individuals:
list.snippet: Take extra precautions with pregnant women, young children, and individuals with weakened immune systems.

list.title: Hygiene:
list.snippet: Maintain good hygiene practices, such as washing hands frequently, to minimize any potential exposure.

list.title: Listen to your body:
list.snippet: Pay attention to any side effects you may be experiencing and follow your healthcare team's guidance on managing them.

related_questions.question: How long does radiation treatment take?

text_blocks.snippet: Radiation therapy sessions typically last between 10 to 40 minutes, but the actual time the radiation is delivered is only a minute or two. The majority of the time is spent ensuring proper positioning and setup. The entire treatment course can last from a few days to several weeks, depending on the type and location of the cancer.

list.title: Individual Treatment Session:
list.snippet: Each session, where radiation is delivered, is relatively brief, usually a few minutes.

list.title: Total Treatment Time:
list.snippet: The overall treatment duration varies significantly. It can range from a few days to several weeks, with most patients receiving daily treatments on weekdays.

list.title: Factors Influencing Duration:
list.snippet: The length of treatment is determined by the type and location of the tumor, the specific treatment plan, and whether external or internal radiation therapy is used.

list.title: Treatment Planning:
list.snippet: After a simulation appointment, which can take about an hour, it can take up to two weeks for the treatment plan to be finalized.

list.title: Patient Experience:
list.snippet: Patients typically spend about 30 minutes in the treatment room, including setup and positioning, even though the actual radiation delivery is brief.

related_questions.question: What can you not do during radiation treatment?

text_blocks.snippet: During radiation treatment, patients should avoid certain actions to protect their skin, manage side effects, and ensure treatment effectiveness. This includes avoiding exposure to extreme temperatures (heat or cold) on the treated area, using certain skin products, and engaging in activities that could irritate the skin or potentially interfere with treatment.
snippet_highlighted_words: avoiding exposure to extreme temperatures (heat or cold) on the treated area, using certain skin products, and engaging in activities that could irritate the skin or potentially interfere with treatment

list.snippet: Heat and Cold: Avoid using heating pads, ice packs, or hot tubs on the treated area, as these can irritate the skin.
Sun Exposure: Protect the treated area from direct sunlight by covering it with clothing or using sunscreen as recommended by your care team.
Skin Products: Avoid using lotions, creams, perfumes, deodorants, and other skin products without consulting your radiation therapy team.
Shaving: Do not shave the treated area unless specifically advised by your doctor.
Tape and Adhesives: Avoid using tape or adhesive bandages on the treated area.
Scratching: Do not scratch or rub the treated area, as this can cause irritation or infection.
Markings: Do not wash off or scrub away any markings used to target the radiation, according to the Canadian Cancer Society.
Swimming: Rinse well after swimming in a pool, as chlorine can dry out the skin.
Smoking: Smoking is generally discouraged during radiation therapy, especially for head and neck treatments, as it can worsen side effects.

list.title: Specific Diets:
list.snippet: Follow any dietary recommendations provided by your doctor or dietitian, as some foods may exacerbate side effects.

list.title: Alcohol:
list.snippet: Discuss alcohol consumption with your doctor, as it may interact with treatment or worsen side effects.

list.title: Exercise:
list.snippet: Engage in light exercise as tolerated, but avoid strenuous activity that could cause skin irritation or fatigue.

list.title: Dental Care:
list.snippet: If receiving radiation to the head or neck area, see a dentist before treatment for a checkup and any necessary procedures, suggests the Canadian Cancer Society.

list.title: Tattoos:
list.snippet: Consult with your radiation oncologist before getting any new tattoos, as they can interfere with treatment planning.

list.title: Hygiene:
list.snippet: Maintain good hygiene in the treated area, but avoid harsh soaps or excessive scrubbing.

list.title: Rest:
list.snippet: Get adequate rest and manage fatigue, which can be a common side effect.

text_blocks.snippet: Always follow the specific instructions provided by your radiation therapy team, as they will tailor recommendations to your individual treatment plan.

text_blocks.snippet: Radiation therapy is a cancer treatment that uses high doses of radiation to kill cancer cells and stop them from growing and dividing. It can be used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery or chemotherapy. The treatment can be delivered externally (using machines) or internally (placing radioactive sources near the cancer).
snippet_highlighted_words: a cancer treatment that uses high doses of radiation to kill cancer cells and stop them from growing and dividing

text_blocks.snippet: Radiation therapy damages the DNA of cancer cells, preventing them from replicating and leading to cell death. While healthy cells can also be affected, they generally have a greater capacity to repair themselves.

list.title: External Beam Radiation Therapy:
list.snippet: This is the most common type, where radiation beams are aimed at the tumor from a machine outside the body.

list.title: Internal Radiation Therapy (Brachytherapy):
list.snippet: Radioactive materials are placed inside the body, either temporarily or permanently, near the tumor.

list.title: Intraoperative Radiation Therapy (IORT):
list.snippet: Radiation is delivered during surgery, often after a tumor has been removed.

text_blocks.snippet: Radiation therapy is used to treat many types of cancer and can be used at different times during treatment, including before, during, or after surgery. It may also be used to relieve cancer symptoms or treat benign tumors.

list.title: Simulation:
list.snippet: Before treatment, a simulation is performed using imaging scans (like CT or MRI) to pinpoint the exact location of the tumor and surrounding tissues.

list.title: Treatment Planning:
list.snippet: The simulation data is used to plan the radiation beams and ensure they target the tumor while minimizing damage to healthy tissues.

list.title: Treatment Delivery:
list.snippet: Radiation therapy is typically delivered in daily sessions, often over several weeks.

text_blocks.snippet: Side effects of radiation therapy vary depending on the treatment area and individual factors, but can include fatigue, skin changes, nausea, and hair loss. Most side effects improve after treatment is completed.
